body.text: Three Southeast Asian governments will this week sign agreements aimed at creating a system for sharing oil and fuel stockpiles in future emergencies, Nikkei Asia reported yesterday.

According to its report, the scheme will involve the construction of storage facilities for diesel and petrol in Indonesia and Thailand, which the Philippines will be able to purchase during times of crisis. The arrangement will be backed by the Japanese government, which has spearheaded efforts to shore up Asia’s fuel supplies in the wake of the Iran war.

As per Nikkei, the state-owned Philippine oil company PNOC Exploration Corporation will on Saturday sign a letter of intent with tank operators in Thailand and Indonesia. This signing will take place on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Business and Investment Summit in Manila, which will precede the 49th ASEAN Summit and related meetings.

Also on Saturday, the governments of the three nations will also sign an agreement to establish a “ticket-based system” for managing the stockpiles. According to the International Energy Agency, tickets “are stockholding arrangements under which the seller agrees to hold (or reserve) an amount of oil on behalf of the buyer, in return for an agreed fee.” Under this arrangement, the buyer of the ticket “effectively owns the option to take delivery of physical stocks in times of crisis.” During non-crisis periods, tank operators will be able to sell their stored diesel and gasoline as usual.
Such a system has been adopted in other parts of the world, including the European Union, but will be the first of its kind in ASEAN, Nikkei stated.

The initiative is a logical response to the Iran war and obstruction of the Strait of Hormuz, which highlighted Southeast Asia’s heavy dependence on oil and refined fuel imports from the Gulf. The Philippines was hit particularly hard by the oil supply shock, given that Middle Eastern imports make up around 95 percent of its total. As a result, in the initial weeks of the Iran conflict, the Philippines saw the highest increase in petrol prices of any nation in the world, while its oil stockpiles were equivalent to only about 15 to 30 days’ worth of demand.

The shortages prompted President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in late March to declare a “national energy emergency” due to the impacts of the war in the Middle East, and the “resulting imminent danger posed upon the availability and stability of the country’s energy supply.” To cover the shortfall, Manila also increased coal power production, approved the use of dirtier fuels, and received a shipment of oil from Russia, its first since before the outbreak of the Russia-Ukraine war.

According to the Nikkei report, the stockpile scheme has been advanced by the Economic Research Institute for ASEAN and East Asia, an Indonesia-based international think tank led by Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade, and Industry. The scheme is intended as the first step to the creation of a wider ASEAN stockpile of fuel and crude oil. Laos and Timor-Leste have also expressed interest in participating.

Japan has good reasons to help safeguard Asia’s energy security. Like the Philippines, it is heavily reliant on energy imports, importing around 95 percent of its oil, including fuels refined from Gulf oil in Southeast Asia. Its multinationals also have a strong presence in Southeast Asia and are reliant on the region’s manufacturing supply chains. In April, Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae launched POWERR Asia, an energy cooperation framework with Southeast Asia that will involve both emergency responses to address immediate fuel shortages and maintain Asian supply chains, and structural responses aimed at strengthening the region’s long-term energy resilience.
Japan also spearheads the Asia Zero Emission Community, founded in 2023, which has since pivoted to building up energy stockpiles among its 11 partner nations. These include nine ASEAN member states.

The economic impacts of the Iran war in general, and the question of energy security in particular, are likely to feature on the agenda of the upcoming ASEAN Summit in Manila, as they did at the 48th ASEAN Summit and related meetings in Cebu in May. During the ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ Meeting, Philippine Foreign Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro said that the energy supply shock was an example of how events outside the region could have “immediate and profound effects” on the region’s economies.
“ASEAN needs to strengthen our crisis coordination and institutional readiness,” she said.
